steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Ottoline Brassbuckle, of the Polytechnic. I hold No. 9's keys until it is yours. Twelve hours of steam on that gauge: that is how long the workshop keeps working without you, so you will sleep tonight, like it or not.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Fifty Brass Ingots from the old stock, and I would rather they became spanners than doorstops.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Watching the work does not make it go faster, I am told, but nobody has ever managed not to watch the first one.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: That canister is from Pip Tumbler, who brings Sprocket Row its bills. Pip's canisters are seldom good news; better answered now than in person.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Rats have been at the Row again, and a Brass Spanner is a perfectly respectable thing to hit one with.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Mind your Rations and come back in one piece; I have only just got this workshop aired.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: The rats have paid you in Crowns, and Pip would like some. Short? Rat scrap is worth more than it smells.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: The rats have been at your sleeves already. They carry umbrella silk home for their nests; take ten scraps off them and you have hand-wraps, which is more than you are wearing now.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Hester kept that workbench drawer better than she kept her rent. Clear it before the day is out; my knees are older than the Boiler.

steps.speaker: Professor Brassbuckle
steps.line: Nothing needs watching: the Boiler and the queue keep working while you are away, and the city will have written by the time you return.
